source: Wikipedia (2026 fetch) Einstellung effect (summarising Luchins 1942, 1959; Solomon 1951; Ross 1952)
finding: The current page does contain the Luchins figures the cross-check could not find in its wikitext search: 483 children in the gender section, and a speed-test study with N=98. The primary Luchins 1942 monograph was still not opened (paywalled).
numbers: Gender section: 483 children, boys less Einstellung than girls, significant only with the Dont-be-blind instruction. Speed test N=98: under stress 3 of 98 solved the extinction problem and 2 used the direct method. Rigidity 70% (no stress) vs 98% (stress); extinction failure 58% vs 97%. Mirror maze 89% vs 71% Einstellung; 55% vs 18% failed. Stutterers 58% vs fluent 4% (Solomon 1951). Age (Luchins 1959): 140 fifth-graders, 79 college students, 21 adults; extinction-task effect 68% children, 56% young adults, 69% older adults. Ross 1952: 65% of older adults vs 29% middle-aged failed extinction.
quote: over half used the simplest solution after the warning Dont be blind
limits: Secondary summary of 1942-1959 work. No group sizes for the 1942 water-jar conditions. The 483 and 3/98 figures are now traced to the page but their primary source is unchecked. Many studies on the page have no N.
agent_relevance: The Dont-be-blind warning is a generic nudge and moved only about half of people. A generic reconsider prompt should not be expected to fully clear set in a model either.

source: Wikipedia (2026 fetch) Candle problem (Duncker; Glucksberg 1962; Frank and Ramscar)
finding: Page gives the Glucksberg 1962 incentive design and a 25% to 50% figure for underlining, with no N and no replication listed. It cites Against Informational Atomism rather than the 2003 paper, so the 25/50 versus 23/55 conflict is not settled by it.
numbers: Glucksberg 1962: low-drive group no prize; high-drive group could win $5.00 (top 25%) or $20.00 (best). Within the filled-boxes condition high-drive did worse than low-drive; empty-boxes condition easier, more solvers and faster. Underlining: 25% to 50% (this page). No N given for any study.
limits: Secondary. No raw means or N. Does not list any replication or failed replication.
agent_relevance: Keeps K02 and K03 at single-source. The incentive effect is only a filled-box effect, so do not generalise pressure hurts to the agent.

finding: Confirms 23% / 55% / 47% for Frank and Ramscar (Stanford undergraduates, no N) and 67% relative gain for McCaffrey 2012. States Adamson 1952 found empty-box participants 2x more likely to solve. Lists no replication failures and no LLM work.
numbers: Frank and Ramscar: 23% original instructions, 55% noun phrases underlined, 47% nouns underlined. McCaffrey: +67% relative. Solomon 1994: 266 freshman science students, 2x2 design with 5 groups. Adamson 1952: empty box about 2x as likely to be solved.
limits: No sample sizes for the key studies. German and Defeyter 2000 (5-year-olds no fixedness, 7-year-olds yes) has no counts.
agent_relevance: Supports using 23 vs 55 as the working figure for layout and wording effects until the 2003 paper is opened.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (mARC-QA), Sci Rep 15:39426
finding: Peer-reviewed version of M-ARC. Items are built to exploit Einstellung. Most models score under 50%; the best were reasoning or large models but still below five physicians.
numbers: Physicians (n=5) 66%, SE 5.3. Best models: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 50%, o1 48%. Several models at or below chance (under 20%). Average over 15 runs per model, 95% CI by bootstrap. All prompts used chain-of-thought.
limits: Only five physicians. Models are early-2025 vintage. Public release of the items in 2025 means later models may have seen them. Chain-of-thought used for all, so no no-CoT control.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models (R1, o1) beat non-reasoning ones by only a few points here. Chain-of-thought alone is not what clears set; compare K19.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate (EMNLP 2024), arXiv 2305.19118
finding: Names a Degeneration-of-Thought problem: once the model is confident, self-reflection cannot produce new ideas. Multi-agent debate (affirmative, negative, judge) helps on counter-intuitive arithmetic, but costs about 2.5x tokens, and the comparison is not token matched to CoT or self-consistency.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive AR (200 items), GPT-3.5-Turbo: base 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0; GPT-4 51.0. Generated tokens relative to CoT: Self-Reflect 1.83x, MAD 2.46x. Common-MT diversity (100 minus Self-BLEU): Self-Reflect 19.3, MAD 49.7; ambiguity-bias error 29.0 vs 24.8.
limits: Dataset built by the authors; single run; models are 2023 GPT-3.5, GPT-4-0314 and Vicuna. Self-consistency at 29.5 may have used fewer tokens than MAD, so a matched-sample comparison could close part of the gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: MAD is an anti-fixation tool in this paper, in contrast to MedEinst where debate agents collapse. The dividing line seems to be forced opposition versus consensus seeking. Moderate disagreement is needed.

source: Liang et al. (2024) arXiv 2305.19118 appendix: debate level and judge findings
finding: The default debate level is 2 (mostly disagreement, a little consensus). Level 0 asked for full consensus on every point. Adaptive early stopping and moderate opposition were both needed; complex items needed more rounds. A weak judge with strong debaters works better than the reverse; different-model judges are not fair.
numbers: Four debate levels (0-3), prompts in Table 11; default 2. Extra generated tokens (Table 12): 1.0x CoT, 1.83x Self-Reflect, 2.46x MAD.
limits: Level-by-level scores are only in a figure; not extracted as text. Authors-built data.
agent_relevance: Explains why consensus-style agent frameworks can amplify the prior (K27). Any multi-agent step in our scaffold must keep a real dissent role and must not be told to agree.

source: MedEinst (2026) Einstellung benchmark for clinical LLMs, arXiv 2601.06636, re-read for gap 4
finding: All 15 plain models and both agents were run zero-shot chain-of-thought. The paper never varies reasoning effort or thinking budget, so it cannot say whether Shidara-style effort lowers the trap rate. The accuracy text-versus-table conflict is still there.
numbers: Text (sec 5.2): GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro base accuracy 54.30% and 53.58%, trap rates above 50%; Gemini trap rate 60.90%. Table 1 trap-rate column values in PDF order: 47.12, 46.12, 47.63, 54.19, 44.88, 43.46, 43.32 | 51.87, 60.90, 42.98 | 36.74, 44.00, 53.88, 66.10, 54.20 | 40.34, 41.69, 33.75. ECR-Agent ablation (Qwen3-32B): base acc 40.25, 55.49, 69.49; robust acc 11.86, 19.94, 24.21; trap rate 43.46, 38.32, 33.75 (none, +DCI, +DCI+CGME). The authors say failure persists in DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B.
limits: PDF text order does not let the baseline-accuracy column be mapped to model names with confidence. Authors prose and table disagree. Data are LLM-generated and LLM-filtered. Code not yet released.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for the effort question. What is shown: a structured scaffold (intuitive top-5 plus an objective problem restatement, then evidence audit) cut the trap rate on one base model from 43.46 to 38.32 with the first module and 33.75 with both, and lifted robust accuracy 11.86 to 24.21. It also adds retrieval, so it is not a clean test of naming alone.

source: Illusion of Insight (2026) appendix C.5 Reasoning shifts at scale, arXiv 2601.00514
finding: Closes part of gap 5: the authors also ran DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o (not only small Qwen and Llama) with the same strict detector. Shifts are still a small minority and do not raise accuracy.
numbers: G=8 traces per item, temperatures 0, 0.05, 0.3, 0.7, 1. MATH-500 and RHOUR: 4,000 traces per model per temperature; XWORDS: 130 items, 1,040 traces. Shift rate MATH-500: R1 4.70-5.17%, GPT-4o 1.45-4.40%. XWORDS: R1 0.96-1.83%, GPT-4o 2.98-7.31%. RHOUR GPT-4o 1.45-3.12% (R1 RHOUR missing). Closest case GPT-4o MATH-500 T=0.3: accuracy with shift 0.632 vs without 0.649. Qwen 1.5B to 7B or Llama 8B did not raise prevalence.
limits: Detector needs a lexical cue plus an LLM-judged plan change, so it misses unlexicalised reframing. GPT-4o is not a reasoning model. No Claude, Gemini or GPT-5 class. R1 RHOUR not run.
agent_relevance: Model size up to R1 scale does not make spontaneous reframing common or useful. External gating (S1/O6 forced by the scaffold) is the only mechanism with positive evidence (+8.41pp, K23).

source: Tian et al. (2023) MacGyver: Are LLMs creative problem solvers? arXiv 2311.09682, re-read for gap 10
finding: The authors attribute most GPT-4 errors to physical infeasibility rather than fixation. They also say the average human is slightly worse than GPT-4 per attempt, potentially owing to functional fixedness. So the MacGyver gap is not clean evidence of fixation.
numbers: 200 infeasible GPT-4 solutions hand-coded: wrong tool usage 42.4%, not achieving the goal 17.7%. Seven LLMs 35-42% success vs average human 65.1%. Humans do better on household problems (familiar), GPT-4 better on domain-specific ones such as farming and fishing.
limits: No Claude 3+, GPT-4o, o1 or later model was tested. Single run, no CI. Wrong tool usage mixes fixation with missing physical knowledge.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open on newer models but is partly answered: the dominant error is grounding, not fixation. A naming scaffold alone should not be expected to close the gap; add a feasibility check.

source: Overcoming cognitive set bias requires more than seeing an alternative strategy (2022) Sci Rep 12, LS-DS task with eye tracking
finding: Eye tracking in the learned-strategy / direct-strategy task. People look at the shortcut but do not use it. Even after watching a video of the shortcut, 29.4% still did not adopt it. Set is a failure to try, not a failure to see.
numbers: N=67 undergraduates (91% female). In the first block 89.6% did not adopt the shortcut. After video: Informed group N=34 used the shortcut in a mean 65.25% (SD 42.88) of correct trials vs Control (video of familiar strategy) N=33 at 9.12% (SD 25.13). 24/34 (70.59%) Informed vs 3/33 (9.09%) Control used it in more than half of trials; 10/34 (29.41%) Informed never adopted it.
limits: One lab, mostly female undergraduates, one task (not a classic insight problem). Same construct as Luchins but not a replication.
agent_relevance: Key for O6: listing or showing the alternative role is not enough. The operator must force an attempt with the alternative (a test step), not only a mention.

source: Can habits impede creativity by inducing fixation? (2021) Front Psychol, PMC8548374
finding: Frequent past use of an item made idea generation more fluent but less flexible (alternative uses). Individual habit tendency (Slips-of-Action task) did NOT predict Candle Problem success, and predicted only the pyramid puzzle.
numbers: Candle sample 69 after excluding 16 who already knew it (of 85). Binomial model F(1,66)=1.895, p=0.169; latency F(1,66)=0.153, p=0.697; Welch t=0.558, p=0.584. SOAT score solvers 69.83 (SD 17.57) vs non-solvers 64.39 (SD 23.03). Pyramid puzzle t=3.077, p=0.003. Candle time limit 8 min. Task order not randomised.
limits: Small, low power, pictures not real objects (authors say this may underestimate fixation). Few candle solvers, so the null is weak.
agent_relevance: Supports a use-frequency effect in divergent tasks (fluency up, flexibility down), not for the classic candle item. Treat the candle item as low power.

source: Semantic accessibility and experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving (2026) J Intell, PMC13117359
finding: Fixation was dosed in a modified Chinese Remote Associates Task: strong prior reinforcement hurt only when the right answer was weakly associated to the cues. Direct (if small) evidence that memory strength sets fixation size (gap 8, in humans).
numbers: N=30 (24 female, mean age 21.2), within-subject 2x2 (accessibility high/low x induction strong/weak), interaction significant. Cue-solution associative frequency high vs low accessibility t(29)=3.63, p<.001, d=0.32. Matched-pair follow-ups (n=15 pairs) not significant (e.g. d=-0.246). Induction vs non-induction trials confirmed that induction created a set.
limits: Small N, native Chinese speakers on a verbal task, one lab, 2026, not replicated. Power analysis said 29 needed.
agent_relevance: Test for the agent: raise the number of in-prompt examples that share a decoy pattern and measure error against how weakly the true answer is associated. Trigger the name-the-fixation step on prior reinforcement in context.

source: Does physical interaction with insight problems really affect the solution rate? (2026) J Intell, PMC13208192
finding: Manipulating physical materials did not help the spatial Pencil (match) problem. A realistic picture that clarified how the misunderstanding arises did help a matchstick arithmetic item. What helps is information that corrects the representation, not action as such.
numbers: Exp 1: 90 students recruited, 87 analysed (39 male, 48 female; 45 STEM, 42 non-STEM); paper vs physical format, no significant difference in success. Exp 2: matchstick arithmetic I=II+II, picture of real matchsticks gave a significant rise in solutions (counts not extracted). Background cited: ring-chain problem 30% vs 3% solved with physical rings.
limits: Exp 2 numbers not read in detail. Italian students, small samples.
agent_relevance: Supports S1 restate that exposes the structure of the misunderstanding. A change of format that does not alter the representation does nothing.

source: The role of motor activity in insight problem solving, nine-dot case (2019) Front Psychol, PMC6352738 (quotes MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle 2001)
finding: Secondary report of MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle (2001) Exp 1: simplified nine-dot variants with stronger hints toward the right first lines were solved by 80-93%, while nobody solved the nine-dot problem itself. Supports a lookahead / progress-monitoring account. Primary QJEP paper (paywalled) not opened.
numbers: 80-93% solved on simplified problems; 0 solved on the nine-dot problem (Exp 1, per this review). Own experiments: finger drawing on a tablet; solvers and non-solvers differed in pause and stroke duration.
limits: Secondary. Weisberg and Alba 1981 (hint to go outside the square) still not opened. Hint-versus-no-hint rates not obtained.
agent_relevance: Nine-dot difficulty depends on how many steps ahead the solver must look. For a model this predicts failure on nine-dot variants needing deeper search regardless of naming; test simplified variants.

source: Crossref and Europe PMC searches for LLM tests of classic fixation tasks (2026-11-03)
finding: Searches for LLM plus Luchins/water-jar, candle, nine-dot, matchstick and functional fixedness found no study that runs the classic tasks on current models. Hits were Naeini 2023, M-ARC, MedEinst and divergent-thinking comparisons only. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited and WebSearch had a shared limit, so the search is incomplete.
numbers: Europe PMC queries returned 0 LLM water-jar, 0 LLM candle, 0 LLM nine-dot papers. Related: Sci Rep 2025 GenAI models outperform students on divergent and convergent thinking (PMC12546817) tests alternative uses and convergent tasks, not fixation.
limits: Absence of evidence under degraded search tools. Preprint servers outside the Europe PMC index were not covered.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2 and 3 remain open and are best closed by our own run: candle, nine-dot and water-jar sequence items to the scaffold at equal tokens.

finding: Page has no experimental data. It cites Maier and Casselman 1970 and Lung and Dominowski 1985 only as studies of difficulty, and does not mention Weisberg and Alba or MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle.
numbers: Mathematics only: 2n-2 segments suffice for n dots (Klamkin 1955, Selfridge 1956).
agent_relevance: No solve-rate base rates from Wikipedia for nine-dot; do not quote any until Weisberg and Alba 1981 is read.
